title: The Uncountable Larder
intro: Un consejo, una información — perfectly countable in Spanish. Advice, information — stubbornly, permanently singular in English. Stock the larder correctly.

A2.why: Spanish “un consejo” is countable; English says “a piece of advice” or “some advice”.

A2.right: tables, chairs, beds — never 'furnitures', say 'a piece of furniture'
A2.why: “Muebles” is plural, but furniture is one mass: “The furniture is new.”

A2.right: suitcases and bags — never 'luggages', say 'a piece of luggage'
A2.why: Count the bags, not the luggage: “three bags” or “three pieces of luggage”.
Spanish has “informaciones”; English only has “information” or “a piece of information”.
Money takes a singular verb: “The money is on the table.”

A2.right: reports of events — takes a singular verb: 'the news is good'
A2.why: News ends in -s but is singular: “The news is good”, “a piece of news”.

A2.right: school tasks to do at home — never 'homeworks'
A2.why: “Deberes” is plural, but homework is uncountable: “I have a lot of homework.”

A2.right: the food made from flour — say 'a loaf of bread', not 'a bread'
A2.why: Bread is a mass: “some bread”, “a loaf of bread” or “a slice of bread”.

A2.right: the white drink from cows — say 'a glass of milk', not 'a milk'
A2.why: Liquids are uncountable: “some milk”, “a glass of milk”.

A2.right: the grain for a paella — never 'rices'
A2.why: Rice is a mass of tiny grains: “The rice for the paella is ready.”

A2.right: songs and tunes in general — never 'a music' or 'musics'
A2.why: Count the songs, not the music: “a piece of music”, “three songs”.

A2.right: what grows on your head — 'her hair is grey', not 'her hairs are'
A2.why: Spanish “el pelo” is singular too: “Her hair is grey.” “A hair” is one single strand.

B1.why: Traffic is one mass of cars: “There was a lot of traffic on the way to Valencia.”

B1.right: tools or machines for a job — never 'equipments'
B1.why: Say “a piece of equipment”, never “an equipment”.
Progress is singular: “The patient is making good progress.”

B1.right: rain, sun, wind, etc. — never 'a weather'
B1.why: No “a” with weather: “What lovely weather!”, not “What a lovely weather!”

B1.right: careful study of a subject — never 'a research'
B1.why: Say “a piece of research” or “a study”, never “a research”.
Knowledge has no plural, though “a good knowledge of Spanish” is fine.

B1.right: a place to live or stay — never 'accommodations' in British English
B1.why: In British English it is uncountable: “We found accommodation in Ruzafa.”
Scenery is the whole view: “The scenery around the Albufera is beautiful.”

B1.right: good or bad fortune — never 'a luck', say 'good luck'
B1.why: No “a” with luck: “Good luck!”, “a bit of luck”.
Fun is uncountable: “We had a lot of fun at the Fallas.”

B1.right: being allowed to do something — never 'a permission'
B1.why: Ask for permission, not “a permission”: Spanish “un permiso” is the trap.

B1.right: harm caused to something — never 'damages' for harm
B1.why: Damage has no plural for harm; “damages” is money a court orders you to pay.

B2.right: comments on how well something was done — never 'feedbacks'
B2.why: Feedback is uncountable: “some feedback”, “a piece of feedback”.
Count the programs, not the software: “a piece of software”, “two apps”.

B2.right: proof that something is true — never 'evidences'
B2.why: Say “a piece of evidence”; Spanish “evidencias” is the trap.
Machinery is the mass; one is “a machine” or “a piece of machinery”.

B2.right: poems as a genre — never 'poetries', say 'a poem'
B2.why: Poetry is the art; a single text is “a poem”.

B2.right: the people who work somewhere — never 'staffs' for people
B2.why: Staff is the whole group; for one person say “a member of staff”.
Jewellery is the collection; one item is “a piece of jewellery”, or name it: a ring.
Cutlery is uncountable: “Put the cutlery on the table.”
Rubbish is uncountable in British English: “Take the rubbish out.”

B2.right: farm animals such as cattle — never 'livestocks'
B2.why: Livestock is the whole herd: “The ranch’s livestock was sold at auction.”
Say “a round of applause”, never “an applause”.
Clothing is uncountable, clothes is plural; one thing is “an item of clothing”.

C1.why: Expertise is uncountable: “her expertise in surgery”, never “her expertises”.

C1.right: the basic physical systems of a country — never 'infrastructures'
C1.why: Roads, railways and power together: one mass noun.

C1.right: laws as a group — never 'legislations', say 'a law'
C1.why: Legislation is the body of laws; one is “a law” or “a piece of legislation”.

C1.right: recorded film or video material — never 'footages'
C1.why: Footage is uncountable: “some footage”; one short piece is “a clip”.

C1.right: letters or emails exchanged — never 'correspondences' in this sense
C1.why: All the letters together: “His correspondence was published after his death.”
Merchandise is the goods as a whole; one thing is “an item” or “a product”.

C1.right: the leaves of plants collectively — never 'foliages'
C1.why: Foliage is all the leaves together; one is simply “a leaf”.

C1.right: pens, paper and office supplies — never 'stationeries'
C1.why: Stationery with -ery is the supplies; “stationary” with -ary means not moving.
“The cowboy ran out of ammunition”, never “ran out of ammunitions”.

C1.right: wild animals and plants in their habitat — never 'wildlifes'
C1.why: Wildlife is uncountable: “The Albufera’s wildlife is rich.”

C1.right: all the bits and pieces linked to an activity — never 'paraphernalias'
C1.why: A mass noun: “all the paraphernalia of a country doctor’s bag”.

C1.right: a warm welcome for guests — never 'hospitalities'
C1.why: Hospitality is uncountable: “Thank you for your hospitality.”
